questions.stem: A Linux administrator adds a new drive but it does not appear after rebooting. Which file should they check to ensure it mounts at startup?
questions.explanation: /etc/fstab (File System Table) lists all drives and partitions to mount at boot. A drive missing after reboot is typically not listed there.
questions.trap: /etc/hosts maps names to IPs. /etc/resolv.conf configures DNS. Neither is related to drive mounting.

questions.stem: A technician needs to override a DNS entry for a test server so the hostname 'staging.corp.local' resolves to a specific IP on their Linux machine only. Which file should they edit?
questions.explanation: /etc/hosts entries take precedence over DNS. Adding the IP and hostname there will override the DNS server response on that specific machine.
questions.trap: /etc/resolv.conf tells Linux which DNS servers to use - it cannot override specific DNS records.

questions.stem: A Linux file shows the following in ls -l output: -rw-r--r-- professor staff backup.txt. What can members of the 'staff' group do with this file?
questions.explanation: The second set of three characters 'r--' is the group permission. r = read, - = no write, - = no execute. Group can read only.
questions.trap: The first set rwx is for the file owner (professor). Group gets the middle set.

questions.stem: A script file needs to be executable by its owner, readable by the group, and have no access for others. Which chmod command achieves this?
questions.explanation: 740: owner=7(rwx), group=4(r--), others=0(---). Owner can read/write/execute. Group can only read. Others have no access.
questions.trap: chmod 744 gives others read access. chmod 777 gives everyone full access. 740 is the only correct combination.

questions.stem: A Linux technician needs to run a single system administration command with elevated privileges without remaining as root. Which is correct?

choices.text: su -c 'command' to create a root shell
chmod 777 the command, then run it

questions.explanation: sudo runs a single command with root privileges without elevating the entire shell session. Best practice over using su.
questions.trap: su elevates the entire terminal session to root. sudo is preferred for individual commands.

questions.stem: A Linux administrator wants to find all processes currently running on the system and filter them for processes containing the word 'apache'. Which command does this?
questions.explanation: ps -e lists all processes on the system (not just the current user's). Piping to grep filters for matching names.
questions.trap: ps without -e only shows the current user's processes. An apache process running as another user would not appear.

questions.stem: A Linux partition is nearly full. Which command identifies which directories are consuming the most space?
questions.explanation: du -h (disk usage, human-readable) scans the current directory and subdirectories, showing how much space each one uses. df shows how much is free on each filesystem, not where it was used.
questions.trap: df shows free space per filesystem mount point, not per directory. To find what is consuming space, du is the right tool.

questions.stem: A technician wants to query the DNS record for a hostname from the Linux command line and get detailed output. Which command should they use?
questions.explanation: dig is the Linux DNS query utility, functionally equivalent to Windows nslookup but with more detailed output including the question section, answer section, and query statistics.
questions.trap: nslookup exists on Linux too but dig provides more detailed diagnostic output and is the preferred tool on Linux/Unix.

questions.stem: Match each Linux command to its Windows equivalent.
questions.explanation: Cross-platform command equivalents are tested frequently. Know both the Linux name and what it replaces from Windows.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow files are TRUE? Select all that apply.

choices.text: /etc/passwd is readable by all users on the system
/etc/shadow stores the actual hashed passwords and is restricted to root
/etc/passwd shows 'x' in the password field when shadow is in use

questions.explanation: /etc/passwd is world-readable but shows 'x' where the password would be - the actual hashes are in /etc/shadow which is root-only.
questions.trap: (b) is the classic mistake. /etc/passwd does NOT contain actual password hashes when shadow is in use.
